app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — Client-side rejectedEmails is exact-string only and purely cosmetic; an attacker just retries with a case variant or hits the endpoint directly.

app/controllers/users_controller.rb:199 — Response echoes attacker-supplied name/username/email verbatim in `values` and exposes structured `errors`, expanding the reflected surface for anonymous callers.

app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — errors` is a Hash here but an Array in the `RestClient::Forbidden` rescue (line 214) of the same action, so clients get two incompatible shapes for the same key.

app/controllers/users_controller.rb:199 — Only the validation-failure branch returns `errors`/`values`; the StatementInvalid and NicknameUnavailable rescues omit them, so the JS `rejectedEmails` logic silently never fires for a duplicate-email race.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — Any `errors.email` entry (presence, uniqueness/taken, domain not_allowed) is treated as a rejected email and re-labelled with the generic `user.email.invalid` text, hiding the server's actual reason and never telling the user the address is blocked.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — rejectedEmails.contains(email)` is an exact-string match against `values.email`; if the server ever normalizes (downcase/strip) the email before `attributes` is read, the client check will miss and the field shows as valid again.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` on the class prototype is shared across all controller instances rather than initialized per instance.

lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — BlockedEmail.should_block?` mutates `match_count`/`last_match_at` inside a validator, so `user.valid?` followed by `user.save` in users#create double-counts every blocked attempt and any later email edit also bumps stats.

config/locales/server.en.yml:734 — New `user.email.blocked` key exists only in server.en.yml with no client-side counterpart or specific message surfaced to the user (client falls back to `user.email.invalid`).
app/controllers/users_controller.rb:199 — New `errors`/`values` keys in the users#create failure response have no controller spec coverage in this change.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — where(email: email)` is a case-sensitive exact match, so a user signing up with `Bad@Spamclub.com` (or with surrounding whitespace) bypasses a blocked entry stored as `bad@spamclub.com`; normalize with `Email.downcase`/strip before lookup.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — should_block?` performs a `save` (match_count++, last_match_at) as a side effect of validation, so every `valid?`/`save` attempt on a User with a changed email (including repeated failed submits, admin edits, and `create_for_email` paths) inflates the stats rather than counting actual block events.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — Increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write (`match_count += 1` then `save`), so concurrent signups with the same blocked email lose updates; use `increment_counter`/`update_all` instead.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — Return value of `record.save` is ignored and the save runs BlockedEmail validations (extra uniqueness query); a failed save silently loses stats while the block decision proceeds.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:275 — Any server-side `errors.email` (e.g. uniqueness "already taken" or domain not_allowed) pushes the email into `rejectedEmails`, after which the client permanently reports it as `user.email.invalid`, masking the real reason and blocking retry even if the condition changes (e.g. the other account is deleted).

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined on the class prototype, so the array is shared across all instances and is never cleared, persisting rejections across modal opens/sessions.

lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — BlockedEmail.should_block?` is skipped whenever a whitelist/blacklist error already exists but still runs (and mutates stats) even when the value is blank/nil-only-guarded by presence ordering; behaviour depends on validator declaration order in User, which is fragile.

lib/validators/email_validator.rb:1 — EmailValidator` lives in lib/validators but no autoload path addition for `lib/validators` is included in this change; `validates :email, email: true` will raise `ArgumentError: Unknown validator: 'EmailValidator'` unless the directory is already autoloaded.

app/controllers/users_controller.rb:199 — values.email` returns the raw attribute the server stored; if any normalization is later applied to `user.email`, it will no longer equal the client's `accountEmail` and `rejectedEmails.contains` will never match.

db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 — action_type is NOT NULL with no DB default; the default is only applied in the model's before_validation, so raw SQL inserts, imports, or update_all/insert_all-style bulk loads (the documented "manually load the table" use case) will fail with a not-null violation; add default: 0 (:block).

app/models/blocked_email.rb:11 — should_block? does an exact-match WHERE email = ? with no normalisation (no downcase/strip) and no uniqueness validation is case-insensitive, so blocked-list matching is inconsistent with the case-insensitive email semantics used elsewhere.
db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:1 — No db/schema.rb / structure.sql update accompanies the new table, so schema dump is stale for db:schema:load-based setups.

db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:1 — Migration file was previously committed as an empty file (blob e69de29) and later populated; an environment that already ran the empty migration will have its version recorded in schema_migrations and never create the table.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — should_block? performs a write (match_count/last_match_at save) inside validation on every User validate run, causing non-idempotent side effects and a read-modify-write race on match_count under concurrent signups; use increment_counter/update_all.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — should_block?` performs a SELECT plus a full-record UPDATE (match_count, last_match_at, updated_at) as a side effect of validation, so every `valid?`/`save` on a user with a changed email issues a write; `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` then `user.save` (lines 168/172), double-counting matches and doubling DB round trips per signup.

lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — BlockedEmail.should_block?` is invoked from a validator, so stat-tracking DB writes happen inside every validation pass (including `valid?` calls with no intent to persist); move the counter increment out of the validator into the controller/create path or make the validator read-only.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — Lookup uses exact `email =` while user emails may differ in case; without normalising (e.g. `Email.downcase`) the unique index is hit but matches are missed, and adding a `lower(email)` query later would bypass the index.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — record.save return value is ignored, so a failed BlockedEmail validation (e.g. uniqueness/presence) silently drops the stat update while still blocking.
app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count read-modify-write is not atomic; concurrent signups with the same blocked email lose increments (use increment_counter/update_all).

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — should_block? performs an UPDATE (match_count/last_match_at) on every validation triggered by unauthenticated signup with no rate limiting, allowing attackers to hammer writes on a hot row and inflate stats.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both point out that the block-checking method (`should_block_email?` / `should_block?`) has unintended side effects: it persists changes (increments match_count / updates last_match_at) during what should be a read/check operation, leading to misleading behavior and potential concurrency/statistics issues.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both describe the same core flaw: the email domain regex is not properly anchored/boundary-checked, so it matches domain suffixes and can be bypassed using longer domains/subdomains (e.g., whitelist/blacklist evasion via evil.example.com or gmail.com.attacker.net). Candidate adds extra concerns (regex injection/ReDoS), but the primary issue matches the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — Lookup is an exact-string match and User never normalizes email, so "Bad@Spam.com" or " bad@spam.com " bypasses the block list entirely.

app/models/user.rb:47 — validates :email, email: true` requires EmailValidator to be resolvable but the diff adds no autoload entry for lib/validators, so User validation raises "Unknown validator" on every save.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` defining `EmailValidator < ActiveModel::EachValidator` and changes `User` to use `validates :email, email: true`. Whether this raises "Unknown validator" depends on the app’s autoload/eager_load configuration (e.g., whether `lib` or `lib/validators` is already in autoload paths), which is not shown in this diff. The finding states it will break "on every save" as a certainty, but that is not verifiable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:167 — user.valid?` followed by `user.save` runs EmailValidator twice per request, so match_count is double-incremented and stats are wrong.

adjudication.rationale: The diff for `app/controllers/users_controller.rb` only shows additional JSON fields in the failure response; it does not show (or change) any `user.valid?` followed by `user.save` sequence. While the new `EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (which increments `match_count`) and could be sensitive to double-validation, the specific claim about controller behavior and a double increment per request is not verifiable from the provided diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — Unauthenticated signup attempts increment match_count/last_match_at for any listed address, letting an attacker pump or poison the stats and overwrite last_match_at without rate limiting.

lib/validators/email_validator.rb:14 — Distinct "is not allowed." error (vs. the domain-restriction message) is returned to the anonymous client, acting as an oracle to confirm an address is on the block list.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new blocked-email validation error string `user.email.blocked: "is not allowed."` (config/locales/server.en.yml) and raises it from `EmailValidator` when `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is true (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). In `UsersController#create`, failed creates now render `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and a `message` built from `user.errors.full_messages` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb), which will include that distinct blocked-specific text vs the existing domain restriction text (`user.email.not_allowed`). Since account creation is an anonymous endpoint, this creates an information-disclosure oracle to distinguish “on block list” from other invalid/not-allowed cases.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — Plus-addressing and subaddress variants ("bad+1@spam.com") trivially evade the list; no domain or pattern matching is supported despite "comprehensive" intent.

adjudication.rationale: The new blocking logic only performs an exact match on the full email string (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` in `BlockedEmail.should_block?`), and the validator passes the raw value through (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`). There is no normalization (e.g., stripping `+tag`), nor any domain/pattern matching support. So variants like `bad+1@spam.com` would not match a stored `bad@spam.com`, which is a concrete limitation of the implementation shown, though not necessarily a correctness bug unless broader matching was intended.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — record.errors[attribute].blank?` short-circuit skips should_block? when domain whitelist/blacklist fails, so blocked-email stats are silently not recorded for those attempts.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, the blocked-email check is gated by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. Since the whitelist/blacklist branches above add an error on the same attribute, `should_block?` will not be called in those cases, so `match_count`/`last_match_at` stats in BlockedEmail.should_block? won’t be updated for attempts that already fail domain restrictions. This is a real behavior in the diff, but it’s not clearly a correctness defect unless the intended requirement is to always record blocked-email stats even when other validations fail.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — match_count is incremented even for action_type :do_nothing and even when the User save later fails for unrelated reasons, so counts do not reflect actual blocks.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `BlockedEmail.should_block?` intentionally increments `match_count`/`last_match_at` whenever a `BlockedEmail` record exists, regardless of `action_type` (it only uses `action_type` to decide the boolean return). The accompanying spec explicitly expects statistics to be updated even when `action_type` is `:do_nothing` (`include_examples "when a BlockedEmail record matches"` in both contexts). So incrementing for `:do_nothing` is not a defect per this change, and the claim that counts are meant to reflect only “actual blocks” is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — Read-modify-write on match_count without a lock or `increment_counter` loses updates under concurrent signups.

app/models/user.rb:47 — Validator only runs `if: :email_changed?`, so paths using update_column/save(validate: false) or pre-existing accounts keep blocked addresses; blocking is signup-only despite the PR title.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does gate the new blocked-email logic behind `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in `app/models/user.rb`, so users whose email isn’t being modified won’t be re-checked if the blocked list changes later. However, it’s not strictly “signup-only” because it will run on any email change, and bypassing validations via `save(validate: false)`/`update_column` is generally true for any validator and not specific to this PR.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — Client-side rejectedEmails is exact-string only and purely cosmetic; an attacker just retries with a case variant or hits the endpoint directly.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `rejectedEmails` only as a client-side UX shortcut (JS checks `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and shows `user.email.invalid`). Server-side enforcement is handled by the new `EmailValidator` (`validates :email, email: true`), which checks whitelist/blacklist and `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` and adds an error (`user.email.blocked`). So “hit the endpoint directly” would still be validated/rejected by the server; the finding’s implied security bypass is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:199 — Response echoes attacker-supplied name/username/email verbatim in `values` and exposes structured `errors`, expanding the reflected surface for anonymous callers.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` to the JSON response on failed signup (users_controller.rb). That does echo back request-provided fields and exposes structured validation details to the (potentially anonymous) caller, which increases the reflected payload surface and makes validation outcomes easier to machine-consume. However, from the diff alone this is not a verifiable security defect (it’s just JSON returned to the requester, and the same error information was already present in `full_messages`), so it’s better treated as a review concern about response shape/exposure rather than a confirmed bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — errors` is a Hash here but an Array in the `RestClient::Forbidden` rescue (line 214) of the same action, so clients get two incompatible shapes for the same key.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `users_controller.rb#create` now renders `errors: user.errors.to_hash` (a Hash). However, the finding claims that in a `RestClient::Forbidden` rescue (around line 214) the same key `errors` is an Array, causing inconsistent response shapes. That rescue block and its rendered JSON are not shown anywhere in this diff, so the claimed incompatibility cannot be verified from the provided changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:199 — Only the validation-failure branch returns `errors`/`values`; the StatementInvalid and NicknameUnavailable rescues omit them, so the JS `rejectedEmails` logic silently never fires for a duplicate-email race.

adjudication.rationale: In the JS, `rejectedEmails` is only updated when the server response includes both `result.errors.email` and `result.values.email` (see `create_account_controller.js` new check in the failure callback). In `UsersController#create`, this diff adds `errors:` and `values:` only in the normal validation-failure `else` JSON render. The method still has a `rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` (and the finding mentions other rescues) which, if they return JSON without these fields, will produce inconsistent error payloads and prevent the new client-side `rejectedEmails` behavior from triggering for those failure paths. The claim about a “duplicate-email race” specifically isn’t directly shown in the diff, but the inconsistency across failure paths is.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — Any `errors.email` entry (presence, uniqueness/taken, domain not_allowed) is treated as a rejected email and re-labelled with the generic `user.email.invalid` text, hiding the server's actual reason and never telling the user the address is blocked.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `rejectedEmails` and, when `result.errors.email` is present, pushes `result.values.email` into that list (create_account_controller.js ~274). The email validation computed property then checks `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns `failed: true` with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of whether the server-side reason was `not_allowed`, `blocked`, `taken`, etc. This effectively masks the specific server-side email error for subsequent inline validation. (The PR still flashes `result.message`, which may include the real reason, but the field-level validation is re-labeled as generic invalid.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — rejectedEmails.contains(email)` is an exact-string match against `values.email`; if the server ever normalizes (downcase/strip) the email before `attributes` is read, the client check will miss and the field shows as valid again.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the client stores `result.values.email` (from `user.attributes.slice("...","email")`) and later checks `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` against the current `accountEmail`. adjudication.rationale: The diff adds BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) which, when a blocked_email row exists, increments match_count, sets last_match_at, and saves on every call (app/models/blocked_email.rb:11-18). EmailValidator calls should_block? during user email validation (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), which is exercised during signup. This does introduce write-amplification/lock-contention risk if many requests validate the same blocked email, inflating stats and hammering a hot row. However, the diff doesn’t show whether request-rate limiting exists elsewhere, so “no rate limiting” can’t be fully verified from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — Blocklist check is skipped whenever a domain whitelist/blacklist error already exists and only runs on email_changed?, and is only enforced via model validation (not on other email entry points like invites/auth providers that skip validation).

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email check is explicitly gated by `record.errors[attribute].blank?`, so if the whitelist/blacklist logic already added an error, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` will not run (and thus won’t block or update match stats in that case). The note about it “only runs on email_changed?” is true (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in `app/models/user.rb`), but that was also the case before (the old `email_validator` was also conditional on `email_changed?`), so it’s not a newly introduced defect. The claim about other entry points (invites/auth providers) skipping validation is not verifiable from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:16 — The `record.errors[attribute].blank?` short-circuit is untested: no case where a whitelist/blacklist error is already present and should_block? must not be called (use `expects(...).never`).

The added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only tests `should_block?` returning true/false with no pre-existing email errors, and does not cover the short-circuit behavior (e.g., with `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist` causing an error and asserting `should_block?` is never called). adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — No qunit test for rejectedEmails: neither that a rejected email flips emailValidation to failed nor that a failed createAccount response with errors.email pushes onto rejectedEmails.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is a shared array on the prototype, so rejections leak across controller instances/tests; a test that re-instantiates the controller would expose this and it should be initialized in init().

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` as a controller property in `Discourse.Controller.extend(...)`. In Ember, mutable defaults defined this way live on the prototype and can be shared across instances created from that class, so the finding’s core claim (prototype-shared array risk) is grounded in the diff. Whether it manifests as a user-facing bug depends on how Discourse instantiates/reuses this controller (often controllers are singletons), which isn’t verifiable from the diff alone, so it’s best treated as a real but not conclusively user-breaking issue; initializing in `init()` would avoid cross-instance/test leakage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:20 — No test that should_block? handles nil/blank email or case differences (where(email:) is case-sensitive while user input may be mixed case), so lookup normalization is unverified.

The added spec (spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb) only covers exact-case matching and doesn’t exercise mixed-case input (or any normalization expectation), so whether blocking is intended to be case-insensitive is unverified by tests. The nil/blank aspect is less critical because presence validation runs before the email validator and `EmailValidator` only calls `should_block?` when `record.errors[attribute]` is blank, but the case-normalization gap is a specific, diff-grounded missing edge-case test.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:5 — Validator spec builds a full User record only to call validate_each directly; there is no integration test that `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` on User actually triggers blocking on save (e.g. Fabricate(:blocked_email) then User.create).

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:31 — subject` is memoized and only invoked once per example, so the do_nothing/block contexts never verify that repeated calls keep incrementing match_count or that concurrent increments are not lost (read-modify-write on match_count without increment_counter).

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block? does a non-atomic read/modify/write (`record.match_count += 1; record.save`) after `where(...).first`. Under concurrent calls for the same email, updates can be lost (last write wins), causing incorrect `match_count`/`last_match_at` statistics. The added spec only asserts a single +1 change per call and does not cover repeated/concurrent invocations, so this issue is not caught.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:24 — should be_false` passes on nil because should_block? returns `record && ...`; assert `== false` or make the method return a strict boolean so the contract is explicit.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when no record exists it returns `record && ...`, which evaluates to `nil` rather than a strict boolean `false` (diff: `blocked_email.rb`, `record && record.action_type == ...`). The spec asserts `subject.should be_false` for the non-existent-record case (diff: `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb`), and depending on the RSpec version `be_false` may treat `nil` as acceptable, making the test less explicit about the intended contract. This is a test/clarity issue rather than a functional defect, since `nil` is falsey in Ruby and callers can still use it in conditionals.
